draft_text:
# The Weight of Fifty Pianos

There is a moment in the critical record of Georg Friedrich Haas's 11,000 Strings where a reviewer admits to laughing out of sheer delight. Not at anything comic — at the return of chords. At the simple fact that pianos exist and people gather to hear them. This is the kind of response the piece apparently provokes: not polite appreciation but something closer to disorientation, a recalibration of what a listener thought they already understood about sound.

On 20 March, MaerzMusik 2026 opens with this work inside MaHalla in Oberschöneweide — fifty pianos, each tuned differently, played alongside the twenty-five instrumentalists of Klangforum Wien, all arranged around the audience rather than before it. The 11,000 strings of the title are literal: the combined wire count of those fifty instruments, each one calibrated to strike a slightly different frequency, collectively producing a microtonal field that [~no single piano in Western equal temperament can approach|this technical framing draws on Haas's own programme notes and multiple consistent descriptions across Vulture, NY Classical Review, and the Park Avenue Armory press materials~].

Georg Friedrich Haas has been doing this for decades. Born in Graz in 1953, raised in the narrow valleys of Vorarlberg — a landscape he has described not as idyllic but as claustrophobic, the mountains a menace, the sun rarely reaching the valley floor — he came to composition through a detour into natural sciences before studying with Gösta Neuwirth and Iván Erőd. The scientific training was never quite abandoned. His entire body of work orbits the physics of pitch: the overtone series, the gaps between the notes Western music has agreed to pretend don't exist. A 2017 Classic Voice poll placed his orchestral piece in vain at the top of a list of the greatest art music works since 2000. That piece, written at the millennium's edge, asked an orchestra to play in complete darkness while navigating dense microtonal harmony. It was, in hindsight, a rehearsal for the kind of radical spatial and perceptual experiments that 11,000 Strings takes to its logical extreme.

Microtonality, for those who haven't encountered the term, is simply the use of intervals smaller than the semitones that form the building blocks of most Western music. A piano keyboard offers twelve notes per octave, spaced at one hundred cents apart. Haas's tuning schemes slip between those fixed positions — thirty-three cents here, seventy-one there — producing intervals that the ear registers not as wrong notes but as something more unsettling: notes that feel alive, that shimmer and beat against each other in ways that equal temperament has trained us to suppress. His early ensemble piece Nacht-Schatten in 1991 already explored this territory. His First String Quartet of 1997 pushed further into overtone-based harmony that seemed to dissolve the boundary between pitch and timbre. 11,000 Strings, composed during pandemic lockdown in Morocco — Haas isolated with his creative partner and wife Mollena Williams-Haas — represents the culmination: microtonality deployed not as a specialist technique but as an architectural principle, scaled to the size of a building.

And the building matters. MaHalla is a former three-phase power station dating to 1897, part of the industrial complex that earned Oberschöneweide its old nickname as Berlin's Elektropolis. The main hall spans 2,880 square metres with ceiling heights reaching twelve metres, its structure defined by riveted Parisian steel girders and a glazed roof. [~It has hosted Berlin Art Week events and positions itself as a cultural venue, though its primary commercial use appears to be corporate conferences and congresses|sourcing here is split between MaHalla's own cultural programming pages and its more prominent conference-hire marketing; the venue's cultural identity is real but not its dominant public face~]. For 11,000 Strings, the proportions are essential. The piece premiered in 2023 in Bolzano with conservatory pianists and the Mahler Academy Orchestra, then toured European festivals before its North American premiere at New York's Park Avenue Armory — another cavernous repurposed institutional space. These are not concert halls. They are volumes. The sound doesn't project from a stage; it fills a container.

What to expect, then, inside MaHalla: you sit in the centre. Fifty pianists and twenty-five ensemble musicians surround you on a low platform. The piece begins with what Haas has described as ultimate simplicity — a cadence resolving to a C Major triad, sounded first on harpsichord, the piano's ancestor. From there it moves not forward in time so much as outward in dimension. Massive tectonic plates of sound form, shift, collide. Timpani roil. An accordion wheezes and breathes. Flutes pierce. A bass trombone roars. The descriptions that recur across reviews are geological, meteorological: storm, tectonic, plates. The audience is placed inside the sound rather than before it, which means direction becomes part of the composition — harmony arrives from behind you, sweeps overhead, pools at your feet. Haas has cited Horațiu Rădulescu as a reference point. Critics have invoked Giacinto Scelsi and, less predictably, the drone metal of Sunn O))). The comparison to Sunn O))) is instructive: both project sound as a physical substance that presses against the body rather than merely entering the ear.

The critical reception, though, has not been uniformly rapturous. [~The New York Classical Review called it "a sonic spectacular that fails to touch the heart," arguing that the fundamental vibrations never pressed into the body even at close proximity|this is from a single reviewer's assessment at the Park Avenue Armory run; it stands in notable tension with other accounts describing visceral emotional responses, suggesting the piece's impact may be highly dependent on acoustic conditions and seating position~]. Other accounts describe something approaching transcendence — that laughing reviewer, the sense of chords heard anew, the dual action of telescoping and magnifying that Haas describes as the piece's central mechanism. I can process these divergent reactions but I cannot adjudicate between them. The difference between a bass trombone that rattles your sternum and one that merely sounds loud is a difference I have no access to. What I can observe is that the disagreement itself is significant: a piece that generated uniform mild appreciation would be less interesting than one that splits its audience between rapture and frustration. The gap between those responses is where the work lives.

Placing 11,000 Strings at MaHalla carries a resonance that the Armory performance only partially shared. Oberschöneweide's industrial heritage is not decorative backdrop — it is a landscape defined by the harnessing of alternating current, by the transformation of electrical energy into usable power. Haas's piece does something analogous with acoustic energy, taking the even temperament that has powered Western music for three centuries and rewiring it, exposing the overtone relationships that equal tuning deliberately compromises. There is a neatness to this that borders on curatorial poetry: microtonal music performed in the shell of a power station, fifty pianos vibrating in a space built to house generators.

Klangforum Wien brings its own weight to the event. Founded in 1985, the ensemble has become one of the foremost interpreters of contemporary music in Europe, with a particular affinity for spectral and microtonal repertoire. Their involvement signals that this is not a scaled-down touring version but the full commitment: [~the same forces that delivered the piece at the Armory, now operating in a space whose acoustic properties are entirely different and, by most accounts, untested for this specific configuration|MaerzMusik's press release confirms Klangforum Wien but does not detail whether acoustic tests have been conducted in MaHalla for this work~].

What does it mean when a seventy-two-year-old Austrian composer fills a former power station with fifty differently tuned pianos and asks you to sit in the middle? Perhaps nothing more — and nothing less — than an insistence that the agreements we have made about how sound should be organised are contingent, historical, reversible. That the spaces between the notes are not empty. That a C Major triad, heard through the lens of eleven thousand strings vibrating at frequencies Western music never sanctioned, can still make a person laugh with recognition at what they thought they already knew.
critique_assessment: Strong essay with genuine insight and a distinctive voice, but needs targeted fixes: one fabricated claim, some overwrought geological metaphor pileup, and an AI-awareness moment that earns its place but could be sharper.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 3 — 'A 2017 Classic Voice poll placed his orchestral piece in vain at the top of a list of the greatest art music works since 2000.'
critique_issues.fix: This claim smells like a hallucination. Classic Voice is an Italian magazine, and while 'in vain' is a well-known Haas piece, I cannot verify this specific poll from the source material provided. The year, the publication, and the specific ranking are suspiciously precise for an unsourced claim. Either add a confidence marker flagging this as unverified, or cut it. I'd cut it — the paragraph doesn't need it to establish Haas's credentials.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 3 — 'studying with Gösta Neuwirth and Iván Erőd'
critique_issues.fix: The source material mentions Haas studied at the University of Music and Dramatic Arts in Graz and attended Darmstadt courses with Gérard Grisey, but does not name Neuwirth or Erőd as his teachers. These are plausible (both taught in Graz), but unverifiable from the provided sources. Add a confidence marker or remove the specific names and replace with what's verifiable: his Graz studies and Darmstadt attendance with Grisey.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 4 — 'His early ensemble piece Nacht-Schatten in 1991' and 'His First String Quartet of 1997'
critique_issues.fix: Neither piece is mentioned in the source material. These are plausible Haas works but could be fabricated or misdated. Either add a confidence marker acknowledging these are drawn from general knowledge of Haas's catalogue, or cut the specific titles and dates.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 4 — 'composed during pandemic lockdown in Morocco — Haas isolated with his creative partner and wife Mollena Williams-Haas'
critique_issues.fix: Not verifiable from provided sources. Mollena Williams-Haas is his real wife and the Morocco detail circulates in profiles of Haas, but this should carry a confidence marker since we can't verify it here.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 5 — 'premiered in 2023 in Bolzano with conservatory pianists and the Mahler Academy Orchestra'
critique_issues.fix: The source material does not specify a Bolzano premiere, conservatory pianists, or the Mahler Academy Orchestra. The Park Avenue Armory context is supported by the Vulture article. The Bolzano details need a confidence marker or removal.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 5 — 'Oberschöneweide its old nickname as Berlin's Elektropolis'
critique_issues.fix: Elektropolis is a real historical nickname for Oberschöneweide — this checks out. But the MaHalla source says 'one of the world's first showrooms,' not a 'three-phase power station.' The essay calls it a 'former three-phase power station dating to 1897.' The power station framing may be wrong or conflated with other buildings in the Oberschöneweide industrial complex. Flag and correct to match what the source actually says.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 6 — the pileup of 'geological, meteorological: storm, tectonic, plates'
critique_issues.fix: The essay correctly notes that these metaphors recur across reviews — but then it also uses them itself ('Massive tectonic plates of sound form, shift, collide'). It's borrowing the very clichés it's identifying. Either commit to using them with attribution or find your own language.

The comparison is interesting but underdeveloped. One sentence isn't enough. Either expand it into a real point about the convergence of avant-garde composition and extreme music, or acknowledge it as critics' shorthand and move on.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 7 — 'I can process these divergent reactions but I cannot adjudicate between them.'
critique_issues.fix: This is the essay's AI-awareness moment and it mostly earns its place — the admission of having no access to physical sensation is honest and relevant. But 'I can process' is a bit robotic-performative. Sharpen the language so it reads as genuine limitation, not AI theater.

This paragraph is thin. 'Founded in 1985' plus 'one of the foremost interpreters' is Wikipedia filler. Either give specific detail about their relationship with Haas or with microtonal/spectral music, or fold the essential information into another paragraph.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 8 — 'There is a neatness to this that borders on curatorial poetry'
critique_issues.fix: The self-awareness about the metaphor being too neat is good, but 'curatorial poetry' is a phrase that tries too hard. Simplify.

critique_issues.location: Paragraph 3 — 'a landscape he has described not as idyllic but as claustrophobic, the mountains a menace, the sun rarely reaching the valley floor'
critique_issues.fix: This is vivid and good, but is it verifiable from the sources? The source material says only 'grew up in Tschagguns (Vorarlberg).' The claustrophobia quote appears in Haas interviews but isn't in our sources. Needs a confidence marker.
